Juvenile American lobsters settling from the plankton typically measure approximately 1.3 cm  in total length at the time of benthic settlement, marking the transition from a planktonic larva to a post-metamorphic juvenile. Following this metamorphic event, which occurs at about 90 days after birth  when maintained at a water temperature of 10 °C [T = 10 °C], the young lobsters begin their benthic existence. The energy content of each egg produced by this species is 21 J , a value derived from calorimetric measurements of freshly spawned clutches. This modest caloric investment per offspring reflects the substantial fecundity that female lobsters can achieve; for example, a female with a total length of 18 cm can produce approximately 3,000 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = approximately 3,000 eggs per clutch], a rate that has been documented under stable thermal conditions.

By the end of their first year, juvenile lobsters reared at 10 °C [T = 10 °C] attain an average total length of 3.1 cm , though field surveys indicate substantial variability, with individuals ranging from 2.5 to 3.8 cm depending on local food availability and microhabitat quality. This length increment during the first growing season represents a critical establishment phase, as juveniles must secure adequate shelter and foraging opportunities to sustain their rapid somatic growth. Wet weight at six years of age for individuals maintained at 10 °C [T = 10 °C] has been measured at 450 g , a value consistent with growth curves derived from mark-recapture studies in the Gulf of Maine. This weight gain reflects the cumulative effect of successive molts, each representing a discrete ecdysis event that allows for substantial increase in body dimensions. The relatively slow attainment of this mass compared to some other decapods is likely a consequence of the cold waters that characterize much of this species' geographic range.

Sexual maturation in Homarus americanus involves a complex interplay of size and physiological readiness, with the total length at puberty recorded at 17.7 cm [Lp = 17.7 cm]. In terms of carapace length, which is a more standardized metric for this species, two distinct values have been reported depending on the population and methodology: one study documented a carapace length at puberty of 8.1 cm [Lp = 8.1 cm], while another independent assessment gave a value of 4.4 cm [Lp = 4.4 cm], suggesting either different interpretation of the pubertal molt or genuine geographic variation. The time since birth at puberty for lobsters raised at 10 °C [T = 10 °C] is approximately 5 years [tp = approximately 5 years], a duration that places them among the slower-maturing decapod crustaceans. This delayed onset of reproductive activation is thought to be an adaptation that allows individuals to reach a size sufficient for successful mating and for females to carry a substantial clutch.

The wet weight at puberty differs markedly between the sexes, reflecting the distinct energetic demands of their respective reproductive roles. For females, the wet weight at puberty averages 413 g [Wwp = 413 g], a body mass that supports the development of fully yolked ova and the subsequent brooding of the fertilised eggs beneath the abdomen. Males, by contrast, reach puberty at a considerably lower wet weight of 70.4 g [Wwp = 70.4 g], a difference of nearly six-fold that underscores the pronounced sexual dimorphism in this species. At the other end of the size spectrum, the wet weight at metamorphosis from the larval to the post-larval stage is remarkably low, measured at just 0.0746 g , indicating that the overwhelming majority of growth occurs after the benthic settlement. The ultimate wet weight that a fully grown adult can achieve has been documented at 20,000 g [Wwi = 20,000 g], making Homarus americanus one of the heaviest known decapod crustaceans, corresponding to an ultimate total length of 110 cm [Li = 110 cm] in the largest recorded individuals.

The maximum reproductive rate has been quantified for individuals of different sizes under controlled conditions. At a total length of 18 cm and a temperature of 10 °C [T = 10 °C], the daily reproductive output is approximately 8 eggs per day , while a much larger individual measuring 45 cm in total length at the same temperature of 10 °C can produce an estimated 205 eggs per day  at 10 °C [T = 10 °C], representing a more than twenty-fold increase in fecundity with body size. The maximum documented lifespan for this species at 10 °C [T = 10 °C] is approximately 60 years [am = approximately 60 years], a longevity that far exceeds that of most other crustaceans and that allows for multiple reproductive events across decades. This extended lifespan, combined with indeterminate growth, means that the largest and oldest females contribute disproportionately to the overall egg production of a population, a life-history pattern that has important implications for fisheries management and conservation of the species.
